issues.legal_issue: Under the rule governing information supplied by an accused in custody, the fact discovered is not equivalent to the object recovered, and only information distinctly related to the discovered fact is admissible.
material_facts: An accused in custody stated that he had concealed a firearm beneath a heap of wood behind an old house.
Police found the firearm at the stated location.
Other evidence established that the firearm had been used in the attack.
issues.conclusion: The discovered fact was that the accused knew the firearm was concealed at that location, not merely the recovery of the firearm; the rule in Pulikuri Kottaya remained binding and the High Court was wrong to depart from it.
issues.legal_principle: Section 27 of the Evidence Act operates as a proviso to Sections 25 and 26, permitting the admissibility of the portion of an accused’s statement that distinctly relates to a fact discovered as a result of information supplied in custody. Discovery of a fact cannot be equated with recovery or production of an object, though recovery may help establish the fact discovered. The Court reaffirmed Pulikuri Kottaya v. Emperor, AIR 1947 PC 67, which it said had been repeatedly approved by this Court, including in Jaffar Hussain Dastagir v. State of Maharashtra, State of Rajasthan v. Bhup Singh, Shamshul Kanwar v. State of U.P., and State of Maharashtra v. Damn. It also relied on State of Bombay v. Chhaganlal Gangaram Lavar, AIR 1955 Bombay 1, for the principle that a precedent remains binding unless a superior court takes a different view.

predicates.custodial_disclosure_case: The case concerns information supplied by an accused while in custody.
predicates.accused_identified_a_concealed_object_lo: The accused stated that an object was concealed at a particular location.
predicates.police_found_object_at_that_location: The police found an object at the location identified by the accused.

issues.definition: When an accused in custody identifies where an object is concealed and police find it there, only the information distinctly related to the fact thereby discovered is admissible.

issues.legal_issue: A participant in a joint lethal attack may be held liable for a death caused by another participant when the attack was carried out in furtherance of their shared intention.
material_facts: The accused arrived with other armed assailants, chased the deceased and an injured witness, and fired a lethal weapon during the joint attack.
The accused’s bullet struck the surviving witness, while other assailants’ shots killed the deceased.
The High Court had convicted the accused of murder with a provision concerning unlawful assembly, and the Supreme Court substituted the basis of shared intention.
issues.conclusion: The Court upheld the accused’s murder conviction and sentence, correcting the basis of liability to shared intention with the other assailants.
issues.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code applies where an accused acts with others in furtherance of a common intention; the fact that the accused’s own shot injured a survivor rather than killing the deceased does not prevent liability for the death caused in the joint attack. The Court relied on the circumstances showing the shared intention and replaced the High Court’s reliance on Section 149 with Section 34.

predicates.appeal_against_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal against a criminal conviction.
predicates.accused_joined_a_joint_lethal_attack: The accused took part with others in chasing the victims and using lethal weapons against them.
predicates.accused_and_assailants_shared_an_intenti: The circumstances show that the accused and the other assailants acted together with a shared intention to carry out the attack.

issues.definition: When an accused appeals a conviction after joining a joint lethal attack carried out with a shared intention, the accused is liable for the death caused in that attack.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court should not overturn an acquittal when the trial court’s view is reasonable on the evidence.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted two accused who had carried knives or swords but did not attack either victim or cause them harm.
There was no evidence that those accused knew of the other assailants’ design.
The High Court reversed the acquittals, but the Supreme Court found the trial court’s view reasonable.
issues.conclusion: The Court set aside the convictions and sentences and restored the acquittals.
issues.legal_principle: An appellate court may not interfere with an acquittal where the view taken by the trial court on the facts is reasonable. On the evidence here, the presence of weapons, without action against the victims or evidence of knowledge of the other assailants’ design, did not make the trial court’s view unreasonable.

predicates.appeal_after_acquittal_reversal: The proceeding challenges a conviction entered after an appellate court reversed an acquittal.
predicates.trial_court_view_was_reasonable: The trial court’s assessment of the evidence was a reasonable one.
predicates.evidence_did_not_show_participation_or_k: The evidence did not show that the accused acted against the victims or knew of the other assailants’ design.

issues.definition: When an appellate court has reversed an acquittal despite a reasonable trial court view and the evidence does not show participation or knowledge of the attack, the acquittal must be restored.

issues.legal_issue: A difference between eyewitness accounts of the direction of a shooting and the apparent direction of the resulting injuries does not by itself discredit the eyewitnesses when the victim could have turned during the attack.
material_facts: The eyewitnesses said that the deceased was running forward and was shot from behind.
The injuries could also have been caused by shots fired from the front.
The Court considered it possible that the deceased turned reflexively as the shots were fired.
issues.conclusion: The discrepancy did not justify doubting the eyewitness testimony.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the possibility that the deceased turned during the attack meant that the apparent direction of the injuries did not rule out the eyewitness account. It therefore was not, by itself, a sufficient reason to reject the testimony.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal against a conviction.
predicates.eyewitnesses_described_shots_from_behind: The eyewitnesses said the victim was shot from behind while moving away.
predicates.injuries_could_indicate_shots_from_the_f: The injuries were also consistent with shots fired from the front.
predicates.victim_could_have_turned_during_the_atta: The victim could have turned while the attack was taking place.

issues.definition: When eyewitnesses describe shots from behind but the injuries could indicate shots from the front and the victim could have turned, the discrepancy alone does not discredit their testimony.
